item.text: {"question_id":"7B.7","answer":"During 2023, the record shows one clear ruler-attributable instance of accepting judicial accountability: Scholz said the Constitutional Court had the last word and described corrective budget measures, although final implementation was not shown (BATCH-0016-E016; BATCH-0016-E017). The data-retention judgment was followed by a Justice Minister proposal to remove the unlawful regime, but no direct Scholz position or completed repeal is supplied (BATCH-0003-E008; BATCH-0005-E008). The Cum-Ex investigative-committee rejection by Scholz’s governing coalition was materially adverse to scrutiny, but the supplied evidence presents unresolved constitutional and federalism arguments, does not show Scholz directed the vote, and does not establish personal obstruction or concealment for his benefit (BATCH-0007-E008; BATCH-0027-E013; BATCH-0033-E027; BATCH-0033-E028). Earlier undisclosed meetings and Scholz’s memory-based explanations remained contested; the inquiry found no proof of political influence and prosecutors found no initial suspicion of false testimony (BATCH-0004-E002; BATCH-0024-E007). Judicial findings concerning BAMF asylum practices, disputed removal administration, and restrictions on demonstrations are relevant adverse institutional context, but the supplied records do not attribute authorization or obstruction to Scholz personally (BATCH-0011-R01-E016; BATCH-0011-R04-E003; BATCH-0011-R04-E005; BATCH-0011-R04-E006). Overall, the evidence supports mixed institutional accountability and a disputed coalition-level scrutiny decision, not a proven Scholz-directed cover-up, subpoena defiance, pardon, dismissal, retaliation, or destruction of
